subject: Covariate (species) specific abundance estimates in R

messages.author: 6785f90f57f3fdda
messages.subject: Covariate (species) specific abundance estimates in R
parts:
Greetings, 

I am new to distance sampling and have a question about getting species specific estimates of abundance when you have multiple species in your survey (line transect). I attached some data and an R file that illustrates my question. In my example, there are two species: duck and goose. There are many goose observations, but not as many duck observations. In R, I have chosen the best model, and therefore have a detection function based on all observed species. My question is how do I go from that point to getting an estimate of the abundance of ducks only. Sorry if this is a very basic question. I'm glad this group exists. 

Sincerely, 
Landry Johnson

messages.author: 5caaf011fe45f4d4
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariate (species) specific abundance estimates in R
parts:
Hi Landry, all,

I am really glad you asked this question - I am also struggling with multiple-species distance sampling and  species specific estimates.

As Landry, we have collected multiple-species distance data in a forest fragment in Ecuador, specifically, from spider monkeys, howler monkeys and capuchin monkeys. However, number of sightings of  spider monkeys is less than 40, which hampers the use of Conventional Distance Sampling. We were thinking we could pool howler (>60) and spider monkey's sightings data to obtain a common detection function that could be applied to both howler and spider monkeys (both species have similar detectability). Another idea we came up with is to obtain a detection function using howler monkey data only, and to use it for both howler and spider monkeys. In addition, we are also considering using data from spider monkeys groups not encountered along transects to estimate the detection function. Could you please let us know which method would be more accurate?

Thank you for all your help, we really appreciate it.

Best regards,

Irene

messages.author: 9dce01a6123da978
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariate (species) specific abundance estimates in R
parts:
Hi Irene and Landry,

It may not surprise you to learn that there is no one-size-fits-all answer to your question. If you have two species with similar detectability then a pooled detection function should work fine. But because usually in this situation one or more of the species we want to pool has few detections associated with it, we typically have limited data to show this. This means you are making a judgement call, the validity of which depends on your understanding of the relevant species, habitats, survey methods etc.

That said, it's still worth looking at how distributions for the different species compare with one another. If you see evidence of different detectability even with your limited sample, you should be cautious about using a pooled function. One thing to be aware of, when making these comparisons, is cluster size. I imagine this is an important factor to take account of when estimating detection functions fit monkeys. In which case detectability should ideally be compared between groups of similar size. 

Building a detection function just using data for the common species is probably a good idea for estimating densities of the common species. However, I can't think of an advantage of excluding spider monkey data from the detection function aimed at estimating densities of spider monkeys.

Using non-survey spider monkey detections to boost your sample sizes for detection functions is a good idea. Just be careful that the detections in question were made in similar habitats and circumstances, so that adding them to your dataset is valid. For example, if your transects are all along forest tracks, then adding detections from forest edges (where detectability might be greater) or from off-piste ramblings in the forest interior (where detectability might be lower) is likely to be problematic.

Best wishes, 

Mark

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariate (species) specific abundance estimates in R
parts:
Irene/Landry

Sorry to provide such a brief response (actually teaching a distance sampling workshop at the moment).

I suggest you consider using "species" as a covariate in your detection function, that way you are borrowing strength from both species to inform the general shape of detection function, using the "species effect" to deflect the shape to account for differences between species.  Then use species ID as "Region.Label" to produce species-specific abundance estimates.

Irene/Landry

Let me be less flippant in my answer to your question.  We're developing software to do what you want at the minute.  You'll want to download new versions of mrds and Distance:

remotes::install.github("DistanceDevelopment/mrds")
remotes::install.github("DistanceDevelopment/Distance")

You can then fit a detection function model with species as a covariate.  Following that, you can produce species-specific estimates using a new function introduced to Distance called dht2 according to the following syntax:

the argument model  is the object resulting from your call to ds() , and flatfile  is the name of the object into which you read your survey data. The stratification  argument indicates that the stratification criterion is at the level of the individual detection.

Hope that explanation is a bit more thorough.

Thanks, 

Mark

messages.author: 6785f90f57f3fdda
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariate (species) specific abundance estimates in R
parts:
Hello, 

Thank you all for the input. Eric, the dht2 function is exactly what I was looking for, thank you very much! I appreciate you taking time from the distance sampling workshop you are currently at. 

Mark, from what I understand the correct use would be your latter scenario (if you are going for species level estimates). If differences between detectability are small between two (or more) similar species, the observations from them can be pooled to get a detection function. There should of course be some kind of evidence or expertise to support that assumption. The dht2 function then provides a straightforward way to use the detection function you estimated from both or multiple species and get species level abundance estimates.  

-Landry

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariate (species) specific abundance estimates in R
parts:
Mark

I don't have rules of thumb for number of detections.  However, the idea is that there is a common "key function" shape to the species detection functions.  The information necessary from the 'rare' species is to estimate the "deflection effect": the amount by which the shape of the rare species is deflected from the shape of the common species.

It's the same approach as is applied when using group size as a covariate in the detection function:  groups of all sizes share the same detection function shape, but the rate of degradation in detectability changes between size categories as shown here:

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covariate (species) specific abundance estimates in R
parts:
Thanks Eric, that is helpful. I guess (based on little more than instinct) that you'd want to at least be into double figures (ideally upwards of 20?) before estimating a deflection effect. And obviously you'd want to be fairly sure that carrying over the same basic key function from the commoner species was justifiable. So probably not a good idea when you think detection might vary wildly between species? 

Have a good weekend, 

Mark

On Fri, 23 Aug 2019, 17:45 Eric Rexstad, <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:

Mark

I don't have rules of thumb for number of detections.  However, the idea is that there is a common "key function" shape to the species detection functions.  The information necessary from the 'rare' species is to estimate the "deflection effect": the amount by which the shape of the rare species is deflected from the shape of the common species.

It's the same approach as is applied when using group size as a covariate in the detection function:  groups of all sizes share the same detection function shape, but the rate of degradation in detectability changes between size categories as shown here:

On 22/08/2019 21:47, Mark Wilson wrote:
Hi Eric,

The new capability to fit a detection model with spp covariate sounds useful. Do I understand correctly that this allows one detection function model to accommodate different species, with differences in detectability? If so, are there any minimum per-species sample size recommendations? I can't see how detectability could be reliably specified for a species with very few detections. Or should the use of this approach on datasets where one or more species are represented by small samples be limited to situations where one suspects that inter-specific differences in detectability are small? 

Thanks, 

Mark 


On Thu, 22 Aug 2019, 21:17 Eric Rexstad, <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:
Irene/Landry

Let me be less flippant in my answer to your question.  We're developing software to do what you want at the minute.  You'll want to download new versions of mrds and Distance:

remotes::install.github("DistanceDevelopment/mrds")
remotes::install.github("DistanceDevelopment/Distance")

You can then fit a detection function model with species as a covariate.  Following that, you can produce species-specific estimates using a new function introduced to Distance called dht2 according to the following syntax:

the argument model  is the object resulting from your call to ds() , and flatfile  is the name of the object into which you read your survey data. The stratification  argument indicates that the stratification criterion is at the level of the individual detection.

Hope that explanation is a bit more thorough.

On Aug 22 2019, at 6:03 pm, Eric Rexstad <er...@st-andrews.ac.uk> wrote:

Irene/Landry

Sorry to provide such a brief response (actually teaching a distance sampling workshop at the moment).

I suggest you consider using "species" as a covariate in your detection function, that way you are borrowing strength from both species to inform the general shape of detection function, using the "species effect" to deflect the shape to account for differences between species.  Then use species ID as "Region.Label" to produce species-specific abundance estimates.

On 22/08/2019 06:23, Irene Duch Latorre wrote:
Hi Landry, all,

I am really glad you asked this question - I am also struggling with multiple-species distance sampling and  species specific estimates.

As Landry, we have collected multiple-species distance data in a forest fragment in Ecuador, specifically, from spider monkeys, howler monkeys and capuchin monkeys. However, number of sightings of  spider monkeys is less than 40, which hampers the use of Conventional Distance Sampling. We were thinking we could pool howler (>60) and spider monkey's sightings data to obtain a common detection function that could be applied to both howler and spider monkeys (both species have similar detectability). Another idea we came up with is to obtain a detection function using howler monkey data only, and to use it for both howler and spider monkeys. In addition, we are also considering using data from spider monkeys groups not encountered along transects to estimate the detection function. Could you please let us know which method would be more accurate?

Thank you for all your help, we really appreciate it.

Best regards,

Irene

Missatge de Landry Johnson <landryjo...@gmail.com> del dia dc., 21 d’ag. 2019 a les 19:59:
Greetings, 

I am new to distance sampling and have a question about getting species specific estimates of abundance when you have multiple species in your survey (line transect). I attached some data and an R file that illustrates my question. In my example, there are two species: duck and goose. There are many goose observations, but not as many duck observations. In R, I have chosen the best model, and therefore have a detection function based on all observed species. My question is how do I go from that point to getting an estimate of the abundance of ducks only. Sorry if this is a very basic question. I'm glad this group exists. 

Sincerely, 
Landry Johnson
